Simulation study: do the weights recover known effects?

Source: vignettes/articles/simulations.Rmd
simulations.Rmd

This article checks, by simulation, whether the new features of ipw do what they should: each scenario generates data in which the true causal effect is known, estimates it, and repeats this hundreds of times, in the spirit of the simulated example in the JSS paper (van der Wal & Geskus 2011).

Main findings

  • The new weights remove confounding when their model is correct. Naive analyses and weights from misspecified models are biased by 13% to over 100%; the new weights reduce this to under 6% in every scenario but one (8% for smooth terms in ipwtm(), scenario 5b).
  • The remaining small biases (1 to 6%) are properties of inverse probability weighting, not of the implementation. Weights computed from the true model (oracle weights) have the same bias for log-normal and gamma doses and for counts, and for smooth terms and ordinal exposures the bias shrinks as the sample grows.
  • A bootstrap that re-estimates the weights gives accurate standard errors when the weights are well behaved, where the variance from robust standard errors is 1.22 to 1.25 times the true variance (model-based SE 10 to 12% too large). It does not fix analyses with extreme weights: with poor overlap or long products of time-varying weights, no standard error reaches 95% coverage, and the bootstrap is then not better than the robust standard error.

How the results were produced. The study is in dev/simulation-study.R; the code below shows the essential lines of each scenario. It takes about 20 minutes on 4 cores, so this page shows saved results. To reproduce them, run Rscript dev/simulation-study.R in the package folder (seed 20261101), or start the simulations workflow from the GitHub Actions tab. Each replication has its own L’Ecuyer random number stream, so the results are the same for any number of parallel workers and on Windows (where the replications run one after another); only different versions of R or of the packages used could change them slightly. Replications: 500 for scenarios 1 to 4, 250 for 5 and 6, 200 for the large-sample and oracle checks, 1000 for 7a and 7b, and 500 for 7c and 7d, each with 200 bootstrap samples.

Reading the tables. Bias is the mean estimate minus the truth. The MCSE (Monte Carlo standard error) shows how precisely the simulation estimates that bias: a bias within about 2 MCSE of 0 could be simulation noise. Empirical SD is the spread of the estimates; RMSE combines bias and spread.

Oracle weights are computed from the true model that generated the exposure, which is known only in a simulation. They show what weighting achieves without any error in estimating that model: if oracle weights have the same bias as the estimated weights, the bias comes from weighting itself, not from the model.

1. ATE, ATT and overlap weights

The effect of a binary exposure varies with the confounder l, so the three estimands differ. Their true values, from 2 million simulated people, are ATE = 1.00, ATT = 1.27 and ATO = 0.86. Each weighting scheme is compared with its own target. Weights from the true propensity scores (1 / probability of the observed exposure) are oracle weights.

d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$a <- rbinom(1000, 1, plogis(0.5 + 0.8 * d$l))
d$y <- d$a * (1 + d$l) + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.att <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  denominator = ~ l, data = d, estimand = "ATT")$ipw.weights
coef(lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = w.att))["a"]
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted (target ATE) 0.999 1.983 0.985 0.005 0.114 0.991 500
ATE weights 0.999 1.002 0.003 0.004 0.089 0.089 500
ATT weights (target ATT) 1.275 1.281 0.006 0.005 0.106 0.106 500
ATO weights (target ATO) 0.861 0.864 0.003 0.004 0.079 0.079 500
true probabilities, 1 / den (ATE) 0.999 1.007 0.008 0.007 0.148 0.148 500

All weighted estimates are within 1% of their own estimand; the unweighted difference is twice the ATE.

2. Skewed continuous exposures: gaussian, gamma or log-normal

One unit of dose raises the outcome by 1. In 2a the dose is log-normal given l, in 2b gamma. Oracle weights divide the true marginal density by the true conditional density. For the log-normal dose the marginal has a closed form; for the gamma dose it is the average of the true conditional density over the sample’s values of l. In 2a they are also computed for a 5 times larger sample.

d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(2000))
d$dose <- exp(0.5 + 0.5 * d$l + rnorm(2000, 0, 0.6))   # 2b: rgamma(2000, 3, 3 / exp(0.5 + 0.3 * d$l))
d$y <- d$dose + 2 * d$l + rnorm(2000)
w.ln <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "lognormal", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
oracle <- dlnorm(d$dose, 0.5, sqrt(0.61)) / dlnorm(d$dose, 0.5 + 0.5 * d$l, 0.6)
# 2b: f <- function(x, l) dgamma(x, shape = 3, rate = 3 / exp(0.5 + 0.3 * l))
#     oracle <- rowMeans(outer(d$dose, d$l, f)) / f(d$dose, d$l)

2a. Log-normal dose

Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.535 0.535 0.002 0.044 0.537 500
gaussian weights (misspecified) 1 1.130 0.130 0.006 0.134 0.186 496
gamma weights (misspecified) 1 0.981 -0.019 0.007 0.154 0.155 500
lognormal weights (correct), n = 2000 1 1.055 0.055 0.005 0.107 0.120 500
lognormal weights (correct), n = 10000 1 1.022 0.022 0.007 0.092 0.095 200
lognormal weights, truncated 1% 1 1.181 0.181 0.002 0.038 0.185 500
oracle weights (true densities), n = 2000 1 1.056 0.056 0.005 0.113 0.126 500
oracle weights (true densities), n = 10000 1 1.022 0.022 0.006 0.091 0.094 200

Log-normal weights remove most of the confounding (unweighted bias 54%). The 5% that remains is the same for oracle weights (5.5% vs 5.6% at n = 2000, 2.2% vs 2.2% at n = 10000), so it does not come from estimating the model: it is the finite-sample bias of weighting with densities of a skewed exposure, whose density ratios have a heavy tail, and it shrinks slowly as the sample grows. The gaussian model is clearly worse, and in 4 of 500 replications gave infinite weights, which ipwpoint() refuses. Gamma weights, the wrong skewed family here, have a small bias but about 1.5 times the spread. Truncation reduces the spread a lot but adds bias.

2b. Gamma dose

Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.758 0.758 0.002 0.038 0.759 500
gaussian weights (misspecified) 1 1.148 0.148 0.003 0.075 0.166 500
gamma weights (correct) 1 1.043 0.043 0.004 0.098 0.107 500
lognormal weights (misspecified) 1 1.025 0.025 0.009 0.204 0.205 500
oracle weights (true densities) 1 1.049 0.049 0.005 0.117 0.127 500

Gamma weights reduce the unweighted bias of 76% to 4.3%; gaussian weights leave 15%. As in 2a, oracle weights have a similar bias (4.9%), so it comes from weighting with a skewed exposure, not from estimating the gamma model. Log-normal weights, the wrong skewed family here, again have a small bias but twice the spread.

3. Count exposures: Poisson or negative binomial

Each extra unit of a count exposure raises the outcome by 0.5. In 3a the counts are overdispersed (negative binomial); in 3b they are Poisson. Oracle weights are computed as for the gamma dose, with the true probability of each count.

d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$v <- rnbinom(1000, size = 2, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$l))   # 3b: rpois(1000, exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$l))
d$y <- 0.5 * d$v + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.nb <- ipwpoint(exposure = v, family = "negbin", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
f <- function(v, l) dnbinom(v, size = 2, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * l))   # 3b: dpois(v, exp(0.5 + 0.4 * l))
oracle <- rowMeans(outer(d$v, d$l, f)) / f(d$v, d$l)

3a. Overdispersed counts

Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 0.5 0.670 0.170 0.001 0.022 0.171 500
poisson weights (misspecified) 0.5 0.328 -0.172 0.003 0.077 0.189 500
negbin weights (correct) 0.5 0.506 0.006 0.002 0.035 0.036 500
oracle weights (true probabilities) 0.5 0.508 0.008 0.002 0.038 0.039 500

Negative binomial weights, the correct model, are within 1.5% of the truth, and oracle weights have a similar small bias (1.6%). Poisson weights over-correct as strongly as the unweighted analysis under-corrects.

3b. Poisson counts

Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 0.5 0.806 0.306 0.001 0.028 0.307 500
poisson weights (correct) 0.5 0.505 0.005 0.003 0.062 0.062 500
negbin weights (also valid: theta large) 0.5 0.515 0.015 0.003 0.063 0.065 500
oracle weights (true probabilities) 0.5 0.511 0.011 0.003 0.070 0.071 500

Poisson weights, now the correct model, are within 1.5% of the truth. Oracle weights do no better (bias 2.2%, with a larger spread): weights from an estimated model are often more precise than weights from the true model (Hirano, Imbens & Ridder 2003), so the estimated weights lose nothing. The negative binomial model remains usable for Poisson data (bias 3.0%), so it is the safer choice when in doubt.

4. Curved propensity: smooth terms with mgcv

The probability of exposure depends on l through a sine curve; the true effect is 2. Oracle weights use the true propensity.

d <- data.frame(l = runif(2000, -2, 2))
e <- plogis(2 * sin(1.5 * d$l))                        # true propensity
d$a <- rbinom(2000, 1, e)
d$y <- 2 * d$a + 3 * sin(1.5 * d$l) + rnorm(2000)
w.gam <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ s(l), data = d)$ipw.weights
oracle <- ifelse(d$a == 1, mean(d$a) / e, (1 - mean(d$a)) / (1 - e))   # stabilized
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 2 4.542 2.542 0.004 0.086 2.543 500
linear logistic weights (misspecified) 2 2.657 0.657 0.004 0.083 0.662 500
s(l) weights, n = 2000 2 2.066 0.066 0.003 0.063 0.091 500
s(l) weights, n = 10000 2 2.032 0.032 0.002 0.027 0.042 200
oracle weights (true propensity), n = 2000 2 2.001 0.001 0.007 0.148 0.148 500
oracle weights (true propensity), n = 10000 2 1.997 -0.003 0.004 0.061 0.061 200

A straight-line logistic model leaves a quarter of the confounding bias. With s(l) the bias is 3.3% at n = 2000 and 1.6% at n = 10000: it halves as the sample grows five-fold, as expected for a smoothing estimate that approaches the true curve. Oracle weights are unbiased, which confirms that the remaining bias comes from estimating the curve.

5. Time-varying exposure, type = "all"

5a. Ordinal dose

A dose level (0, 1, 2) is chosen at each of 4 visits from a proportional-odds model given the confounder L and the previous dose. L is affected by the previous dose and by an unmeasured U that also affects the outcome; the outcome rises by 1 per unit of cumulative dose. This is the situation in the JSS paper where ordinary adjustment fails.

for (t in 1:4) {
  l <- U + 0.4 * prev + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
  dose <- findInterval(0.8 * l + 0.6 * prev + rlogis(n), c(0, 1.5))   # 0, 1, 2
  prev <- dose
}
y <- cumulative.dose + 2 * U + rnorm(n)
w <- ipwtm(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
           numerator = ~ dose.lag, denominator = ~ dose.lag + l,
           id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
# oracle: true probability of the observed dose, multiplied over visits
w.oracle <- ipwprobtm(den = long$p.obs, id = long$id, timevar = long$time)
# weight at the last visit, then lm(y ~ cumulative.dose, weights = ...)
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.491 0.491 0.002 0.035 0.493 250
regression adjustment for L 1 0.856 -0.144 0.002 0.030 0.147 250
ordinal weights (correct), 500 people 1 1.031 0.031 0.007 0.110 0.114 250
ordinal weights (correct), 2500 people 1 1.010 0.010 0.005 0.076 0.077 200
multinomial weights, 500 people 1 1.015 0.015 0.008 0.121 0.122 250
oracle weights, ipwprobtm() with true probabilities, 500 people 1 1.013 0.013 0.010 0.156 0.157 250
oracle weights, ipwprobtm() with true probabilities, 2500 people 1 1.007 0.007 0.006 0.089 0.090 200

Both naive analyses are biased (+49% and -14%). Ordinal and multinomial weights recover the effect; the 3.1% bias of the ordinal weights at 500 people falls to 1.0% at 2500. Oracle weights, from ipwprobtm() with the true probability of each observed dose, are within 1.5%, which also checks that ipwprobtm() multiplies the ratios correctly over time.

5b. Smooth terms in ipwtm()

A binary exposure is chosen at each visit with a curved effect of L (logit = -0.3 + 2 sin(1.5 L) + 0.6 × previous exposure), in the same design.

w <- ipwtm(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit", numerator = ~ a.lag,
           denominator = ~ a.lag + s(l), id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.662 0.662 0.004 0.061 0.665 250
linear logistic weights (misspecified) 1 -0.111 -1.111 0.031 0.489 1.213 250
s(l) weights 1 1.083 0.083 0.015 0.243 0.256 250

Here a straight-line model is worse than no weighting at all: its weights turn the effect of +1 into a negative estimate. With s(l) the bias is 8.3%, the largest of any correctly specified model in this study; with a binary exposure at 4 visits and 500 people, part of the curve rests on few observations.

6. Recurrent exposure events, family = "survival", type = "all"

6a and 6b. Weights against the true weights

Exposure events (for example new prescriptions) happen repeatedly with a known proportional hazard: baseline 2 per unit time, log hazard ratio 0.5 for a fixed covariate x and -1 for a time-varying covariate xt. Because the true hazard is known, the true weights are known too. In 6a all people share a grid of 10 intervals (as in haartdat); in 6b the events happen in continuous time, xt changes at different times for each person, and each event ends an interval (start-stop data cut at events, as in Graffeo et al. 2018).

w <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", denominator = ~ x + xt,
           id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "all", data = d)
coef(w$den.mod)
median(abs(log(w$ipw.weights / true.weights)))
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
Cox coefficient of x 0.5 0.499 -0.001 0.005 0.084 0.084 250
Cox coefficient of xt -1.0 -1.010 -0.010 0.007 0.117 0.118 250
median |log(estimated / true weight)| 0.0 0.072 0.072 0.001 0.022 0.075 250
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
Cox coefficient of x 0.5 0.494 -0.006 0.006 0.087 0.087 250
Cox coefficient of xt -1.0 -0.998 0.002 0.007 0.104 0.103 250
median |log(estimated / true weight)| 0.0 0.090 0.090 0.001 0.021 0.093 250

The Cox coefficients are unbiased in both designs, and the estimated weights are typically within 7 to 9% of the true weights, which is the estimation noise of the baseline hazard.

6c. Causal effect of the number of exposure events

Exposure events happen in continuous time with hazard 1.5 exp(0.6 L). L is updated at 4 visits, is lowered by earlier events (as treatment raising CD4 lowers the need for more) and depends on an unmeasured U that also affects the outcome. The outcome rises by 1 per event.

w <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l,
           id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "all", data = d)
# weight at each person's last row, then lm(y ~ number.of.events, weights = ...)
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.794 0.794 0.004 0.062 0.796 250
regression adjustment for L 1 1.214 0.214 0.003 0.045 0.219 250
survival type all weights 1 1.008 0.008 0.014 0.224 0.224 250

The weights reduce the bias from 79% (unweighted) and 21% (adjustment for L) to 0.8%. The method of Graffeo et al. uses, for an interval ending in an event, the probability of an event during that interval; this simulation shows that the approximation works for estimating a causal effect.

7. Standard errors: bootstrap, robust and naive

Standard errors are judged on the variance scale (Morris, White & Crowther 2019): the variance ratio is the mean estimated variance, mean(SE²), divided by the empirical variance of the estimates (1 is ideal). The model SE, sqrt(mean(SE²)), is shown next to the empirical SE, the standard deviation of the estimates, with the relative error in the model SE, 100 × (model SE / empirical SE − 1), and its Monte Carlo standard error (Morris et al., Table 6). Variances are compared rather than standard errors because a correct variance estimator is unbiased for the variance, while its square root underestimates the standard error on average (see “How the simulations judge a standard error” in the methods article). The tables also give the coverage of 95% confidence intervals. The bootstrap re-estimates the weights and the MSM in each of 200 bootstrap samples (function boot_sim() in the script). The estimates and standard errors of every data set are saved in simulation-se-replicates.rds.

7a and 7b. Linear MSM for a binary exposure

True effect 10, n = 500, stabilized weights. In 7a, exposure probabilities are mostly between 0.1 and 0.9 (good overlap); 7b is the simulated example of the JSS paper, where many people are almost certain to be exposed or unexposed.

msm.effect <- function(dd) {
  w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit", numerator = ~ 1,
                denominator = ~ l, data = dd)$ipw.weights
  coef(lm(y ~ a, data = dd, weights = w))["a"]
}
boot.est <- replicate(200, msm.effect(d[sample(nrow(d), replace = TRUE), ]))
sd(boot.est)                          # bootstrap standard error
quantile(boot.est, c(0.025, 0.975))   # percentile interval
Method Mean estimate Empirical SE Model SE Variance ratio Relative error in model SE, % (MCSE) Coverage of 95% CI MCSE of coverage Replications
bootstrap, percentile CI 10.031 0.481 0.494 1.05 +2.7 (2.3) 0.945 0.007 1000
bootstrap SE, Wald CI 10.031 0.481 0.494 1.05 +2.7 (2.3) 0.955 0.007 1000
robust SE (svyglm), Wald CI 10.031 0.481 0.538 1.25 +11.9 (2.5) 0.972 0.005 1000
Method Mean estimate Empirical SE Model SE Variance ratio Relative error in model SE, % (MCSE) Coverage of 95% CI MCSE of coverage Replications
bootstrap, percentile CI 11.055 1.848 1.317 0.51 -28.8 (2.4) 0.575 0.016 1000
bootstrap SE, Wald CI 11.055 1.848 1.317 0.51 -28.8 (2.4) 0.596 0.016 1000
robust SE (svyglm), Wald CI 11.055 1.848 1.276 0.48 -30.9 (2.0) 0.600 0.015 1000

With good overlap the bootstrap standard error is accurate (variance ratio 1.05, relative error in the model SE +3% (MCSE 2), Wald coverage 95.5%), while the robust variance is too large (variance ratio 1.25, model SE +12% (MCSE 3), coverage 97.2%), in line with Austin (2016); percentile intervals cover slightly less than 95%. In the JSS example the estimate itself is biased (11.1 instead of 10) and all standard errors are much too small (variance ratio 0.48 to 0.51, model SE -31 to -29%), so coverage is 60% or less whatever method is used.

7c. Weighted Cox MSM

Austin (2016) studied weighted Cox models. Here event times are exponential with hazard 0.1 exp(-0.7 a + 0.8 l), censored at 5; n = 1000. The true marginal log hazard ratio, -0.619, is computed from both potential outcomes of 200,000 people (it differs from -0.7 because hazard ratios are not collapsible).

Method Mean estimate Empirical SE Model SE Variance ratio Relative error in model SE, % (MCSE) Coverage of 95% CI MCSE of coverage Replications
naive SE (coxph), Wald CI -0.617 0.11 0.117 1.14 +6.5 (3.4) 0.958 0.009 500
robust SE (coxph), Wald CI -0.617 0.11 0.121 1.22 +10.5 (3.5) 0.968 0.008 500
bootstrap SE, Wald CI -0.617 0.11 0.110 1.00 +0.0 (3.2) 0.940 0.011 500
bootstrap, percentile CI -0.617 0.11 0.110 1.00 +0.0 (3.2) 0.928 0.012 500

All three standard errors are close to the truth here. The bootstrap standard error is accurate (variance ratio 1.00); the robust variance is again too large (variance ratio 1.22, model SE +10% (MCSE 4)) and the naive one somewhat too large (1.14, model SE +7% (MCSE 3)), as Austin (2016) found. All Wald intervals cover the truth in 94 to 97% of samples, so with stabilized weights and good overlap the choice matters little in this setting.

7d. Time-varying exposure, bootstrap by person

The design of scenario 5 with a binary exposure; the bootstrap resamples people with all their visits, and each sampled copy gets a new id.

boot_sim(long, tv.effect, id = "id", R = 200)
Method Mean estimate Empirical SE Model SE Variance ratio Relative error in model SE, % (MCSE) Coverage of 95% CI MCSE of coverage Replications
bootstrap by person, percentile CI 1.047 0.226 0.158 0.49 -29.9 (3.3) 0.722 0.020 500
bootstrap by person SE, Wald CI 1.047 0.226 0.158 0.49 -29.9 (3.3) 0.744 0.020 500
robust SE (svyglm), Wald CI 1.047 0.226 0.175 0.60 -22.4 (3.3) 0.798 0.018 500

Neither method is adequate here: the variance ratio is 0.49 for the bootstrap and 0.60 for the robust standard error (model SE -30% (MCSE 3) and -22% (MCSE 3)), with coverage of 74% and 80%. The weights are products over 4 visits, so a few people get very large weights and the estimate has a heavy-tailed distribution that 500 people do not represent well, the same problem as in 7b. Truncation, a larger sample or a better-balanced design would be needed; the bootstrap does not repair it.

Conclusions

The simulations support the new models: with the correct model, each of them removes nearly all confounding, and the small biases that remain are either shared by weights from the true model or shrink with the sample size. They support a bootstrap that re-estimates the weights for analyses with well-behaved weights, where it gives accurate standard errors and robust standard errors were conservative in these scenarios (binary point treatment, Cox model). They also show its limit: when weights are extreme (poor overlap, long products of time-varying weights), no standard error is reliable, and the first step is to examine the weights (summary(), ipwplot()) and consider overlap weights, truncation or a different model.

References

  • Austin PC (2016). Variance estimation when using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with survival analysis. Statistics in Medicine 35, 5642-5655.

  • Hirano K, Imbens GW, Ridder G (2003). Efficient estimation of average treatment effects using the estimated propensity score. Econometrica 71, 1161-1189.
  • Li F, Morgan KL, Zaslavsky AM (2018). Balancing covariates via propensity score weighting. Journal of the American Statistical Association 113, 390-400.
  • Morris TP, White IR, Crowther MJ (2019). Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods. Statistics in Medicine 38, 2074-2102.
